title: Relationships: Not a Separate Goal, but a Fruit of and a Means to the Goal
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teachers asking whether to spend class time on relationships or on curriculum are asking the wrong question. Using the image of a Mount Everest trek, he claims community forms as a byproduct of pursuing a shared, daunting goal together, not through ice-breakers or autobiographical projects. He therefore budgets no class time for relationship-building and dives into the work, while still doing small things in the first month such as learning names within a week and tracking moments of genuine connection. Think-pair-shares and early pop-up debates let students get to know one another along the way. His emphasis in the early weeks is communicating who the class is and what it is working toward.
points: The choice between relationships and curriculum is a false one, because relationships are a byproduct of working together toward a hard goal.
Stuart skips multi-day ice-breaker and autobiography activities and starts with real academic work from the first activity.
Small deliberate practices (learning names within a week, tracking moments of connection, reflections) still build relationships.
Early classroom structures like daily think-pair-shares and pop-up debates let students get to know each other through the work.
quotes: When people set off on a Mount Everest trek (says the guy who has, of course, done this many times), they don't spend an hour doing relationship-building games, or multiple hours creating “This is Who I Am” projects. Instead, they set off on the trek, and as the peak comes into view, their sense of community coheres around that shared, daunting, thrilling goal. They develop relationships as a byproduct of working toward this challenging thing together.

So I don't really budget class time for the developing of relationships. Even our very first activity is just as much about introducing argumentative claims as it is relationship-building, and that's about as ice-breakery as it gets. No multi-day autobiographical activities — we just dive into the work, no big sharing time.

But relationships aren't the objective in any of this stuff — they are the byproducts of the big objective, of us getting closer together as Everest comes into view. Front and center during those first weeks, I'm trying to communicate, in any way that I can, who we are and what we're working toward.

In the AP class for ninth graders, we're working toward not just a test in May during which the odds say we're supposed to fail — we're also working toward becoming the kind of people who flourish long-term. In the non-AP class, we're working toward mastering world history.

We're all on the same team, in the same family, working toward the same, important thing: becoming the best people we can be. And along the way, the relationships come: in all their joy and mess and substance and utility and goodness.
